text: What tormented Ivan Ilyich most was the lie, accepted by everyone around him, that he was only ill and not dying, and that he needed nothing more than rest and medicine to recover. <break time="0.8s" /> Only Gerasim, a fresh faced young peasant who had come to serve in the house, did not lie, and he performed even the most unpleasant tasks for his master lightly and without any sign of disgust. <break time="0.8s" /> When Ivan Ilyich found that his pain eased if his legs were raised, Gerasim sat for hours holding them on his shoulders, and in that position the sick man found a comfort that no doctor had given him. <break time="0.8s" /> When his master apologized for the trouble, Gerasim answered with a calm smile, We will all die someday, so why should I not take a little trouble for you. <break time="0.8s" /> Ivan Ilyich understood that Gerasim alone pitied him, and he longed, though he was ashamed to admit it, to be petted and comforted like a sick child, which was exactly what no one else would do. <break time="0.8s" /> One evening his wife and daughter, dressed in their finest clothes, came in to see him before going to the theater, where a famous French actress was performing, and their healthy, perfumed presence felt like an insult. <break time="0.8s" /> Later, alone in the dark, he wept like a child over his helplessness, his loneliness, and the cruelty of people and of God, demanding to know why he had been made to suffer so much. <break time="0.8s" /> Then, as he grew quiet, he seemed to hear the voice of his own soul asking what he really wanted, and he answered that he wanted to live, to live well and pleasantly, as he had before.
